title: Termite Inspection Tennessee: A Seller's Guide to WDO
description: How termite inspection Tennessee sellers face works: what a WDO inspection is, where it fits in the sale, and how to handle repairs if something turns up.
body:
If you are selling a home in Tennessee, a termite inspection may come up before you expect it. Buyers and lenders commonly request termite and wood-destroying organism (WDO) inspections here, so it helps to know what the process looks like before an offer arrives.

I am not an inspector, attorney or lender, and this is not legal advice. This post explains how the pieces fit together so you can ask better questions.

## What a WDO inspection is

{{img:0}}

WDO stands for wood-destroying organism. The term covers termites and other pests that can damage the wood in a house. A WDO inspection is a visual check of the home for signs of those pests and for damage they may have caused.

People often say "termite inspection" and "WDO inspection" as if they were the same thing. In everyday conversation they usually are. If a buyer or lender asks for one, ask your agent which one they mean and what the request actually covers.

## Where it fits in the sale

A termite inspection is a common add-on to a standard home inspection. Radon testing and a sewer scope are other common add-ons. It is often paired with a home inspection, so a buyer who schedules the home inspection may also request termite and WDO work at the same visit.

Lenders can also request one, which is why it shows up even when a buyer would not have asked. If the buyer's lender wants it, it becomes part of the path to closing.

It also sits next to your disclosures. Tennessee sellers complete the residential property condition disclosure (or an exemption), and the lead-based paint disclosure applies to homes built before 1978. Answer the disclosure honestly and completely. If you know about past termite activity, past treatment or past damage, talk with your agent about how to describe it accurately. For legal questions about what you must disclose, ask a Tennessee real estate attorney.

Your agent works under the rules of the Tennessee Real Estate Commission, which is the official source if you want to understand how agents are regulated.

## If the report finds something

{{img:1}}

A report that notes activity or damage does not end the sale. It does start a conversation. Here is how that conversation usually goes, in general terms:

1. The buyer's side sends the report, often with a request tied to it.
2. You and your agent review the findings and decide how to respond.
3. The parties reach a written agreement, or they do not.

Repair requests can take different forms, and I will not tell you which one is right for you. Who pays for treatment or repairs is worked out in the contract between buyer and seller, and the answer depends on the findings, the home and the people involved. Before you agree to anything in writing, get written quotes from licensed professionals, and ask your agent to walk through your options.

Two habits help here:

- Read the whole report, not just the summary. Ask questions about anything that is unclear.
- Keep copies of any treatment records, warranties or repair paperwork you have for the home.

## Getting ready before you list

You do not have to wait for a buyer to learn about your home. Some things are worth doing before you list:

- Gather any past termite or pest records, contracts or warranties.
- Look at wood near the ground, crawl space access and areas where moisture collects, and mention anything you notice to your agent.
- Confirm your home's year built. The [Williamson County property search](https://www.williamsoncounty-tn.gov/2099/35739/Property-Data-Search) is one official place to start looking at your property record, which helps you know whether the lead-based paint disclosure applies.
- Decide, with your agent, whether you want to know more about the home before listing.

Older houses deserve some extra attention, since they come with their own questions. I have a separate page on [Franklin older homes](/franklin/older-homes) if that describes yours.

If you want to plan the rest of your sale, the [Free moving checklists](/checklists) are a place to organize the other pieces. For a full picture of the process in town, see [Selling a home in Franklin](/franklin/selling-in-franklin).

## The market is context, not a prediction

Inspection decisions are about your specific house. Still, local numbers help you set expectations about how a sale may go.

In Franklin, Redfin data as of 2026-09-30 (rolling 3 months) shows a median of 55 days on market and 4.0 months of supply. Months of supply is how long it would take to sell every active listing at the current pace of sales. Under 4 months favors sellers, 4 to 6 months is balanced, and over 6 months favors buyers, so 4.0 falls in the balanced range.

For the wider Nashville metro area, Redfin reports a median of 67 days on market for the 4 weeks ending 2026-10-25.

Numbers like these describe what has already happened. They do not predict what your sale will look like, and conditions differ by city, price range and street. You can follow the latest figures on [Market data for the I-65 corridor](/market-data).

## Next steps

If you are thinking about selling, a short conversation can sort out what to do first, including how to handle inspections and any records you already have. Start with [Find out what your home is worth](/sell#form), or reach out through [Contact Scott](/contact) and ask your questions directly.

If you also want to read up on radon, which is another common inspection add-on, the [EPA radon information](https://www.epa.gov/radon) page is the official source.

faq.q: Do I need a termite inspection to sell my house in Tennessee?
faq.a: Termite and WDO inspections are commonly requested by buyers and lenders in Tennessee. Whether one is needed for your sale depends on the buyer, the lender and the contract, so ask your agent early.
WDO stands for wood-destroying organism. A WDO inspection checks a home for signs of termites and similar pests and for the damage they may cause.

faq.q: Is a termite inspection part of a regular home inspection?
faq.a: It is a common add-on to a standard home inspection, along with radon testing and a sewer scope. Buyers often request it alongside the home inspection.

faq.q: What disclosures do Tennessee sellers complete?
faq.a: Tennessee sellers complete the residential property condition disclosure (or an exemption). The lead-based paint disclosure also applies to homes built before 1978. Ask a Tennessee real estate attorney about specific legal questions.
